What follows is still Brother Yuanshen’s own experience, set down still in his own hand; his text reads: On the twenty-eighth of the sixth month of the thirtieth year of the Republic there was a fine rain in the night, and though by morning it had stopped its “spitting,” the sky had still not cleared. I have always been fond of rainy days, and this half-bright, half-clouded weather was besides the freshest, most agreeable day Shanghai had had since the coming of summer; body and mind alike felt at ease. At nine in the morning I stepped out the door and looked up at the sky—one sheet of gloom, a light rain that might drift down at any moment—and so I took my cream-colored raincoat with me.

On Avenue Joffre I boarded a tram, first riding two stops in the wrong direction, then got off, stood waiting at the roadside, and hailed instead a “Yunfei” hire-car to run me straight to the Third Sub-brigade’s quarters at Joffre Terrace. When the car had passed some fifty yards beyond the “Sincere One-Yuan Store” on the right-hand side of Joffre Terrace, I had it stop and walked back; the store had not yet opened, and the passers-by could be counted on the fingers. I looked at my watch: the hands, long and short, stood at nine-forty. I glanced about me, before and behind, and at my leisure stepped into Joffre Terrace.
I climbed the stairs slowly and went into the little back room, where Zhou Xiyuan and Zhu Min were both waiting for me to come. They rose together in welcome, and at once poured me a cup of tea.

Zhou spread once more his boyish smile and said clumsily, “Five minutes yet—it is not ten o’clock.” Then Zhu Min opened the drawer of the writing-desk and took out a sheaf of papers. I leafed through them briefly: within were a two-inch half-length photograph of Xu Liqiu, two sheets of accompanying particulars, and, besides, three or four pages of the “minutes” of the puppet Ministry of Propaganda’s recent conference at Nanjing. How he had come by these so-called “minutes” I could not tell; I should have to go back and look into their “source,” and study their contents closely, before I could judge whether they were genuine or false.

Zhou spoke of the weapons he had been issued in reinforcement—only two revolvers, which he plainly thought too few; he raised again the “suggestions” he had made before, most of them vague enough, and to each I gave him a satisfactory reply. He mentioned too that he had taken on two more reliable action-men, whom he meant first to report for “probation,” and I told him by all means to send their names in. We sat talking some fifteen minutes; Zhu Min, at his side, still said very little. I put the papers away in the inner pocket of my coat, rose to take my leave, and reached for the raincoat I had hung on the wall—at which Zhou too took down his own, a pale coffee-colored one, and said with a smile, “I have another appointment as well; let me walk out with the brigade commander.” Something gave a sudden jump within me, then eased at once: we comrades, for the sake of the work, commonly have a great many appointments, and that today he happened to have business too, and would go out along with me, was ordinary enough, so I thought little of it.

Zhou and I strolled out side by side to the mouth of Joffre Terrace. In no more than twenty minutes the street had already filled with a bustling, jostling crowd. At the lane’s mouth Zhou and I nodded to each other and parted—I westward, he eastward, our backs to one another. I had scarcely turned and gone three steps when all at once I felt two men come running up behind me, seizing me by both arms. Instinctively I struggled, but the two were powerfully built and pinned me the tighter. I looked to left and right: both were burly northern giants, plainly ruffians who had trained in boxing. One of them, a little bald at the crown, lowered his voice at my ear: “No need to take fright—we merely ask you to come and have a talk.” In that instant I understood it all: this was a scheme of “No. 76,” and I had in the end been sold by Zhou Xiyuan, who had got in a step ahead of me. I struggled again with all my strength, and the two braced me the harder, dragging and hauling me to the roadside, where a black sedan stood waiting. Besides the driver there was a pale, beardless middle-aged man, who put his head out of the window and said, “Please get in; we will go and have our talk.” Just then the great thoroughfare was thick with people passing like fish in a stream, and seeing what looked like a kidnapping, not one but was curious; they halted to watch, and in a moment there was a buzz of talk and a wall of onlookers. As luck would have it, directly opposite Joffre Terrace stood a branch of the Bank of China, and at its door were armed guards on duty, who, seeing that something was amiss, came up at once to intervene, drew their pistols to stop the ruffians’ doing, and ordered them to let me go. Finding their design foiled, the ruffians shouted aloud, “He is a robber!” The guards, pistols levelled at the men who had seized me, cried back just as loudly, “Whatever he is, this is the concession, and you may not seize a man as you please!” Clearly these guards were men of sense, who paid no heed at all to the villains’ nonsense. The two ruffians who had done the seizing were forced to release me and stood to one side, able neither to advance nor withdraw, still muttering on. From the sudden fright and my late hard struggling, I sat down on the steps outside the Sincere Company to rest a little, but felt myself drained of all strength, my head swimming, wretched past telling. Lifting my eyes, I saw the onlookers about me growing thicker and thicker; the guard, pistol in hand, watched not only the two ruffians but me along with them. The car of a moment before had long since taken advantage of the confusion to drive off—gone back, no doubt, to carry word. I could not help sighing, and said to myself: “This time I am done for; there is no fleeing now.” For I knew that the power of the enemy and the puppets had long reached into the concessions, and that if they demanded my rendition, the concession authorities were powerless to resist. What now lay before me was no longer the question of my own life or death, but of how to endure the enemy’s and the puppets’ cruel torture, so as to keep the organization safe.

The police sirens wailed long, and the concession patrol cars came very quickly. A police sedan led, and behind it a large “pig-cage van”; reaching the spot, they pulled up with a screech. Four armed constables sprang down one after another, pushed the crowd aside, and shoved me together with the two ruffians into the “pig-cage van,” which bore us away like the wind. Several newsmen would have pressed forward to report, but the constables turned them all back; one of the quicker-handed among them raised his camera, took aim at me, and got off a few shots—and let it go at that. I believed these men would surely follow on to the station house and go on with their reporting, so that news of my arrest would be in the papers by the next day at latest, and District Headquarters would at once take precautionary measures. Thanks to the keen instincts of the Shanghai press, which without knowing it had sounded the alarm for me, and greatly helped in safeguarding the organization, my mind was half at ease.

Before long the car drove into the courtyard of the Lujiawan station house. The constables opened the door and marched us up to the second floor, where they put me and the two ruffians under guard in two separate offices, apart from one another, to await interrogation. The ruffians made a loud clamour, declaring they could not be a step away from me; a “three-stripe head” warder said, “This is our rule here—if he runs off, we answer for it.” It was by now half past two in the afternoon. A plainclothes inspector set to watch me asked me in the Shandong speech what I had done, and added: “I dare say you’ve not had your midday meal? It’s gone two now; I can send someone to order for you—a plate of fried rice, or a bowl of soup noodles. Eat your fill and you’ll have some spirit; an empty belly is no good to anyone.” I saw that he meant it kindly. And bethinking me that I had been trapped by Zhou Xiyuan, that the enemy and puppets had long since fathomed my depth, and that the French Concession authorities plainly had not the power to shield me, but would sooner or later hand me over, I judged there was no longer any need to keep my identity secret here. So I told him plainly that I was a “Chongqing man,” who had through carelessness fallen into a villain’s snare; that “No. 76” had sent men to kidnap me on Avenue Joffre and, failing, I had been brought here. “I am glad indeed to have met a fellow-countryman like you here; I beg you will look after me a little.” Hearing this, he showed deep sympathy, shaking his head again and again to mark his loathing of “No. 76.” Just then another young man in plain clothes came in, seemingly one of his subordinates, and he at once ordered him: “Go and call this Mr. Zhang a Yangzhou fried rice, and bring a bowl of egg-drop soup.” This suited me well, for in truth I was hungry indeed; I took out money and asked him to see to it. Pressing my advantage, I went on to ask the inspector his honored name and of what county he was. I said: “There is no Chinese but loves his own country, and I believe you are the same. It was for the war of resistance, to fight the Japanese devils, that I took up this dangerous work. To be caught in Shanghai, and even to lose my life, was ever within my reckoning, and I do not repent of it in the least. But I have many friends outside who must not be dragged in on my account; so I beg you do me one favor, and whether I live or die from here, I shall be grateful to you for ever. It may be said, too, that you would be doing a favor not to me alone, but to a great many of my comrades, and to the country besides. What say you?” His eyes were on his fellows passing to and fro outside the window, and he said low to me: “You know, my powers are limited, and besides, I eat a foreigner’s rice; the least slip and my rice-bowl is broken. If you ask me to help, I fear it is beyond me.” I said, “I ask only that you put through one telephone call for me—nothing more.” He answered readily: “That much, though it is a risk, I can do; when my man is back with the food, I will call for you.” I pointed to the telephone on the desk and asked, “Can this one not be used?” He waved his hand: “No—that must go through the switchboard; there is a record of it, and someone listening besides.” As he spoke, the food came, and the young detective came in with it. I gave the inspector a look; he took my meaning, called the young fellow over, whispered a while in his ear, then turned back to ask me the number I wanted. I told him outright the number of the internal courier station. The fellow, obedient to his charge, went to the wall telephone across the corridor, took down the receiver, and dialled; luck was with us, and the call went through. He made a sign for me to come and speak, while the inspector stood the whole time at the door to keep watch. The one who answered across the line was indeed Qiu Shuying, chief of the internal courier station. I said hurriedly: “Listen! I am ——; I have been caught, and am held for the present at the Lujiawan station house, with ‘No. 76’ now in treaty for my rendition. You must report to District Headquarters with all speed! Have you understood?” Shuying said she had understood, and then over the line came the sound of weeping. I hung up and went back into the room, thanking the inspector again and again. Then a second thought struck me, and it was ill: the hour for the internal station’s meeting with the District Headquarters courier had already passed for that day, and this news could reach Headquarters at the earliest only by the next afternoon. In a day and a night much may change; now every second counted, and there must on no account be delay.

Much abashed, I begged the inspector to put through one more call, and gave him the number of District Headquarters as well. He looked reluctant, but in the end had his man try again. We were all on edge now; the inspector stood at the door glancing both ways, while I, screened behind him, kept my eyes on the dial, watching the fellow dial digit by digit with his forefinger. He had got through but three numbers when suddenly the inspector gave a call—as if hailing the fellow by name—and the man, quick as an echo, hung up at once: a French officer had come striding past. Only then did I understand that what they most feared was being found letting a prisoner telephone out; for this was an unlawful dereliction of duty, enough to break their rice-bowls and, if it went ill, to land them in court besides—no wonder they were all in a cold sweat. Afterwards this call too went through, and the one who answered was none other than the District secretary, Mr. Qi Qingbin. To him I gave the same brief report, and begged that emergency measures be taken at once against all contingencies. Last of all I declared my resolve: that whether I lived or died, I would pay with my life to guarantee the safety of the organization. Mr. Qi, in his unfailing, unhurried way, said over the line: “Don’t be anxious; deal with it as best you can. We will spare no effort to save you.” I set down the telephone and let out a long breath—a stone, at last, off my heart.

These two telephone calls were to me all but beyond price—and why? First: my being caught was a matter of the gravest moment. In three years’ work in Shanghai I had passed through countless upheavals; I knew most of the comrades, on the inside and the outside alike; in the way of business I had managed intelligence, personnel, action, work of every kind. Up to this very moment, from the District Headquarters at the leading center down to the several groups and brigades, the Kang Corps, and the inner and outer courier stations, five or six in ten had some connection with me; I knew not only all our offices but the man in charge of every unit. Should I fail to bear up under the enemy’s and puppets’ cruel torture, and loosen my tongue but a little, half of “Shanghai District” might be brought to ruin at a single stroke. Second: I recall reading in some book or other that a man’s will, however firm, is yet often overcome by bodily pain—which is why, from of old, there have been past counting the cases of a “confession beaten out.” I hold this a most scientific saying, full of reason. From the very moment of my arrest I had reckoned myself bound to die, and I quoted the saying above to keep myself on guard. In other words, though the road ahead were mountains of knives and seas of fire, I had made my mind fully ready.

Now all was well: these two calls once made, my doubts and fears were wholly dispelled; my cause was just and my spirit bold. I trusted I had ability enough to meet the enemy’s and puppets’ interrogation, and a firm enough will; and even granting the worst—that when it came to it I truly could not bear the torture, and let out the secrets of the organization and its people—I need have no great misgiving, for they had had timely word of the disaster and had long since ordered the changes made to meet it, so that no harm could come. I might set my heart at rest and deal boldly with my own affairs. These two calls once made, then even to die was to die with a mind at ease and eyes that could close—how should I not be grateful?

I heard the two “No. 76” ruffians next door fall to quarrelling again. Before long it came my turn to be brought up for examination, and the Shandong inspector, with another armed guard, took me to the great hall. The hall was packed head to head, most of them criminal offenders. Seeing it would be a good while before my turn came, I stood waiting at the back of the throng. Of a sudden I bethought me of the papers in my pocket, which I must seize the chance to destroy; I drew them slowly out and tore them to shreds behind my back. A plainclothes detective saw me, and I, feigning a fine unconcern, asked him to throw them into the wastepaper basket in the corner; he shook his head and said, “If you want it thrown, throw it yourself.” There was no help for it, so throw it away myself I did. Along the front of the hall ran a row of French windows, and beyond them a large semicircular balcony; as though it were nothing at all, I strolled slowly over—the detectives, of course, still watching me, though they laid no check on my movements. Out on the balcony I leaned on the rail and looked down: below was the station’s front courtyard, with many vehicles standing, two armed police on guard at the great gate, and a throng passing in and out like shuttles. They say a cornered dog will leap the wall; and all at once a notion rose in me—why not seize this chance to jump down and flee? But reckoning it over more closely: the drop was above two zhang, and jumping I should surely break my legs; with guards at the gate and no lack of police in the yard, there was no escaping, and I should only be left a cripple—better not run the risk, the more so as it was of no use. Yet, to tell the truth, I did indeed feel that impulse, and more than once.

A detective came to summon me and took me to another, smaller courtroom to be examined; for what reason I did not know. Within, upon a raised dais, was a long table, and behind it sat a French officer of some forty-odd years, a man of no little depth and gravity. At his side stood a Chinese, whom I guessed to be the interpreter. Below were two armed guards standing in respectful attendance, and the Shandong inspector too stood to one side. Of “prisoners” there was none but myself. I gave the French officer a smiling nod for courtesy’s sake, and he nodded back by way of reply. In his hand he held a small sheaf of papers, turning them over; and glancing down, I saw they were the very documents I had torn up and thrown away in the great hall a while before—retrieved I knew not when, and pieced and patched and pasted into a little booklet. Through the interpreter the French officer first introduced himself: “I am Malone, chief of the criminal section of the French police.” At this a true smile broke from me, for I knew him to be a work-contact of our “Shanghai District”—that is, one of the high inside lines we had placed in the French Concession—though how it had been in the past I did not clearly know, while in these late years he had taken his money and done nothing. (At the time he drew a subsidy of five hundred yuan a month in Chinese notes, whereas my own pay was but eighty-five.) He asked again, “Are you Dai Li’s man?” I answered that I was. The words he said next were very neat: “A man of Mr. Dai’s I cannot but help; but with your affair I truly can be of no help.” I knew that what he said was the plain truth, and gave at once an understanding smile. Then he passed the little booklet through the interpreter for me to see, and said, “This I will not give to them”—meaning the enemy and the puppets—“but will keep myself.” I thanked him. He added: “The Japanese gendarmerie is just now treating for your rendition; about four o’clock you will be able to go. Take care of yourself!” This, after the Shandong inspector, was the second warmth of human feeling that came to me after my being brought to the Lujiawan station house.

It was not yet four when the Japanese gendarmerie and the men of “No. 76” had completed the formalities of rendition. The inspector marched me to the head of the stairs on the third floor; and in a little while there came a heavy tramping down the steps, and a whole crowd descended from above—Frenchmen, Japanese, and more Chinese ruffians besides. A few words passed between them, and one Japanese in plain clothes drew out a pair of bright handcuffs and, with a click, snapped them on my two wrists, then marched me down. In the front courtyard I was put aboard a grass-green Japanese car, which drove out of the station house. To left and right the two ruffians held me fast, as if fearing I might slip away at any moment—though in truth I could not stir a hair. Looking before and behind, I saw a black sedan ahead and a brown one following close, my own car pressed between them, and all bowling swiftly along. The streets we passed at first were ones I knew well; but afterwards the houses and the country to either side grew scattered and forlorn, all strange to me, and I knew we had entered the Chinese city. At last we came to a certain place, and the cars all stopped together; the ruffians hauled me down, and looking up, the first thing to strike the eye and start the heart was a long wooden board hung over the gate, bearing in bold, staring characters: “Hongkou Gendarmerie.” Inwardly I cried, “This is bad!”—now there would be bitterness to swallow. The Japanese in their dealing with “anti-Japanese elements,” and above all with the “Blue Shirt Society,” had ever been cruel past all humanity. Once within the gendarmerie, a man was doomed to nine deaths and one life; the savagery of their tortures was beyond what any man of modern civilization could conceive. Of our own working comrades alone, those who in the Japanese gendarmerie were “not seen alive nor found dead” were more than the fingers could tell. But it had come to this, and I could only harden my scalp and go in with them. At the great gate four short-legged Japanese soldiers in uniform stood bolt upright. Inside the door it was narrow below: on one side a counter, with someone on duty within; on the other, against the wall, a long bench, on which they set me down, and, leaving two men to guard me, the rest went upstairs. My heart was uneasy, not knowing what I waited for. In about half an hour those above came down, and again marched me to a car, and away we sped, coming at last to the infamous puppet Special Operations Headquarters—No. 76, Jessfield Road. Only now did I understand that the halt just past at the Japanese gendarmerie had been but the going-through of a routine form.

The moment I entered “No. 76,” I was taken first to the “High Foreign House.” Two and three at a time, ruffians of somewhat higher standing came in to gaze at me as at some rare show; and presently in came a man in a short suit of white silk, spectacles astride his nose, his face all smiles—not five feet tall, thin and dried-up, for all the world like a monkey. He spoke to me, or seemed to speak to those beside him: “He’s here!”—then introduced himself: “I am Wan Lilang.” I said with a cold laugh, “I have long admired the name; though I do not know you, I have known of you this good while!” By “known of you this good while” I meant the days before he turned his coat and went over to the puppets, when he had been deputy leader of the “Shanghai District’s” Fourth Team; and he seemed to take my drift. He shook my hand and said with a smile, “It’s been a wearying day’s tossing about for you; rest first, and we’ll talk tonight.”

Weighing over my capture, I had been undone by too much self-confidence, and by fancying myself clever; and, more than that, I repented not having heeded Mr. Chen’s words. To be sure, the fact that Bureau Headquarters had been so slow to send back its ruling on the request that Zhou Xiyuan be sanctioned had something to do with it too: it was this that gave Zhou his opening to “strike first and so be master.” Had I but gone straight off, as ordered, to Chengdu for training, there would have been no trouble at all. All this was now past and done; yet to say I felt no after-regret would be false. In a word, my being caught was like missing one’s footing atop a tower ten thousand fathoms high—I had the very feel of being dashed to powder and bits! My work and my future were at an end; my life too was soon to end—and I but twenty-five years old, alas!

Worn out in mind and strength, I yet felt my will to fight burn higher than ever before. In my notebook I secretly wrote two lines: “I swear with my own freedom to buy the freedom of our work; I swear with my own life to safeguard the life of the organization!” Now I was without fear, and must strain my every wit and rouse my every keenness to meet the great trials of the days to come. Die I might, but the “Juntong Bureau” must not die, nor might “Shanghai District” die!

The traitor Zhou Xiyuan had sold me in the broad, brazen light of day, and sooner or later would be brought to the law’s reckoning. Zhu Min’s bearing had been ambiguous throughout—had he, or had he not, been playing a two-man act together with Zhou? And where was he now? This was a riddle lodged in my heart, a knot I could not loose.

Glancing back, I saw on a huge writing-desk in the “High Foreign House” a red visiting-card, pressed beneath the glass top and standing out most sharply to the eye, on which was written this note: “I beg to present two tins of the famous tea ‘Biluochun,’ and humbly entreat that Master Li receive them with a smile. Your junior, Zhu Min.”

This day I felt to be the longest day of my life, and surely the most unforgettable. It bore not only upon my own honor and disgrace, my own gain and loss, but wrought as well, upon the “Shanghai District” that I led, an irreparable and grievous effect, and a debacle past all mending.
On the twenty-ninth of the tenth month of the thirtieth year of the Republic—once midnight was past, it was the thirtieth of the tenth month.

That very night, past eleven o’clock on the twenty-ninth, the telephone rang; and at the first sound of the bell my heart fell to pounding hard. In the past, save for the odd wrong number, no one had ever telephoned my house at such an hour; and if this were no wrong number, it meant there was surely some urgent matter. For of those who knew my home telephone number there were in truth but a very few: one was Brother Hu Yongquan, who had rented this house for me; one was Dr. Nie Chonghou, who had of late been treating my son; and there was Hu Yong’an, who commonly ran small errands for my household, and was Hu Yongquan’s younger brother—none of whom would telephone me in the dead of night. Beyond these, the only one connected with the work was Brother Liu Junqing at the International Settlement police. And Brother Qi Qingbin, the District secretary, closest of all to me, did not so much as know my telephone or my address, so it could not be he. I took up the receiver, and at the single phrase “Is that the Second Master?” I knew already it was Brother Junqing. I said, “It’s me—has something happened?” He said: “Not yet; but it’s very close. The ‘north side’ and the ‘west side’—ten or so have come in, first and last, and they mean to move out in the night. Where to? after whom? That’s not known yet. I’ll not go off duty; there’ll be calls at any time. Take good care of yourself.”

I understood at once: the “Shanghai Japanese Gendarmerie” and the puppet “Special Operations Headquarters” (No. 76) had sent out no small number of men, “giving notice” to the International Settlement police, and were making ready that night for a great round of arrests. Whom would they seize? Most likely of all, ourselves.

In the last few months several of our “Shanghai District” units had come to grief, and no few comrades had been arrested; and even where no man let slip a word of confession, there would yet be left not a few threads to follow. True, what ought to have been dispersed had been dispersed, what ought to have been moved had been moved; yet there was never any wholly sure way to cut every thread clean through and leave no connection at all—the less so when there were sundry ties of person and affair, past all knowing, that could by no means be kept so apart as to have not a single strand to pull upon.

These several days, for the safety and protection of the whole organization of “Shanghai District,” I had indeed done all that lay in my power; yet against this storm now about to break I must of course seek some means of meeting it. So I thought to telephone Old Qi, to tell him first what I had just learned, and to take counsel with him besides. But even as I lifted the telephone the thought struck me—it would not do: he had just moved house, and had no telephone put in yet.

Just at this moment—about one o’clock, past midnight—the telephone rang again; but when I stepped forward two paces to answer, it stopped of a sudden, and taking up the receiver I heard only a buzzing hum. Was this not a mockery? I paced back from the sitting-room to the bedroom to look: the children were all fast asleep, and my wife sat with bowed head on the edge of the bed, knitting wool. I bade her sleep a little earlier; she raised her head and looked, but gave me no answer.

By now it was the dead of night, all hushed and still, and but for the cars that now and again swept past on the main street, there was not a sound. What I most dreaded was the screech of a car halting at the lane-mouth, and some big fellow springing suddenly down—that would be trouble indeed. Truly does suspicion breed its phantoms: with my left hand I caught the lower corner of the window-curtain, with my right lifted a crack of it, and peered out—one sheet of ashen gloom, nothing to be seen. Just as I was going toward the sofa, meaning to sit and think out some plan, the telephone bell rang; and it was Brother Liu Junqing again. He said: “Two or three minutes ago they set out—several parties of them; I am with Clyde now, and the moment there’s word I’ll telephone.” Here he broke off, and thinking he had done I was about to hang up, when of a sudden through the receiver came again the cry of “hello, hello”; I put my ear close and answered, and Brother Junqing went on: “Second Master, one thing more—the French Concession side, they say, is just the same; you had best take particular care.”

Ah, just so—they had gone out in a planned, all-round sweep, and their aim was no small one. What was to be done? I glanced at the clock on the wall: five minutes to two. Outside, the curfew had long been in force, and whatever powers a man might have, at this hour there was no way to bring them into play.

And here I may as well tell over the measures we had taken beforehand. We had long since drawn up a root-and-branch plan to “take the firewood from under the cauldron,” and, once it was sanctioned, were now in the very course of carrying it out. The essential spirit of this plan was the “Great Changeover”: to remove from Shanghai, without exception—whatever a man’s rank, and whether his task were weighty or no—every working comrade whose identity had already been exposed there, or over whom there hung any doubt of safety, and to fill their places with cadres drawn from the several rear areas and from the Loyal and Patriotic Army.

To do this touched matters on far too broad a scale, and the practical difficulties met with in the doing were bound to be many; yet not to do it would not answer either. By our reckoning beforehand, the personnel to be moved out of Shanghai would come to some five hundred all told, a part of them bringing wives and children too; and it was not as with a fighting unit, that at a word of command sets off at once. Those we looked to send to Shanghai, moreover, numbered by the first plan near a thousand, and each of these must be chosen one by one, with even more matters to be weighed than in the case of those moved out; so that the business went forward slowly enough.

There was one most vexing problem, and it is easily guessed—the finding of the funds. For in this great shifting of forces the working premises we gave up—offices, courier posts, points of liaison, wireless, technical stations, and the like—came to more than a dozen; there was the loss besides in furniture, gear, equipment, and fittings; and with a part of the key-money and premiums on the houses not to be got back, the chief accountant and the District accountant, who had the finances in charge, were already crying out under it. And there was, further, a huge sum of travel and transport costs to be found as the need arose, more than the supply could keep pace with.

Where money comes and goes, an account must ever be kept—which was itself a fine irony upon the strict secrecy that secret-service work by its nature demands. Over this very problem we had racked our brains, and had even fallen to disputes, yet in the end must bow to hard fact. And it was just here that the greatest danger lay: should the accounts department one day come to grief, that would be a thing not to be borne thinking of.

I had sat there in the sitting-room turning it over so long, and once my mind touched upon this problem I dared truly think no further. Just past three o’clock the telephone rang again, its sound now shrill and grating, with something in it to set a man trembling and ill at ease. Had it been daytime, or had there been a few more people together, it might have been otherwise. It was, of course, Brother Junqing: “One party has come back to report—they’ve brought in but a single man, and by the look of him he’s not one of ours. I’ll surely stay to the end before I go off; set your mind at rest, Second Master.”

At these words a weight fell from me, and I let go a breath at once. But no longer than it takes to step to the privy and back, Brother Junqing’s first words over the telephone were: “It’s bad! Clyde has just told me—several more parties are back at the station, and ten or so of them are all our people, with a good deal of other stuff besides.” Forcing myself to a show of calm, I begged Junqing to find some way, saying: “Can you look into just who and what they are? The moment there’s word, get a message to me quick.” In less than a quarter-hour, the heart that had but now eased itself was strung tight again. How I chafed! The footing we had, in two years and with such labor, at last brought to some stability, and the foundation of the work built up of the flesh and blood of so many men—was it not all to be undone in a single night? And most maddening of all: there was nothing to do but wait to be beaten, with never room to strike a blow in return.

From half past three, near every ten or twenty minutes there was a call; and the thing I most feared came at last to pass—Brother Junqing said: “There’s one called Cheng Yuan and one called Sun Guochang, two men in the one case; from his house they’ve turned out several trunks of stuff—leases, accounts, and such, they say. I’ve not seen it, and don’t know what it truly is; and now the men from the west side have already taken the two of them off first.”

This Cheng Yuan was none other than the cover-name of the District accountant Chen Xianrong; and Sun Guochang was a kinsman of Chen Xianrong’s, lately called in to help because one man had grown too busy to manage, and already reported and taken on as an assistant. Now here was trouble of the first order: once Chen and Sun came to grief, then whether they held out or no—aye, though they said not a single word—the account-books and vouchers alone were enough to move the whole board.

At this moment my feelings, oddly, grew a good deal steadier than before; over and over I charged myself: on no account lose my head—the great foe was before us, and not the least further slip could be allowed; I must meet it with coolness and nothing less. And so I resolved that two things must be done at once: first, to wire word without delay to Bureau Headquarters in Chongqing; and second, to find Qi Qingbin with all speed and settle upon a plan to meet the change—both to be done at once.

Yet here and now there was not a soul I could send on an errand; to do these two things, I must go myself and none other. Besides this, I had thought too that I might telephone Zhang Zuoxing, and ask him to make a trip to the wireless station and get the telegram off first, then go to Old Qi’s house and call Old Qi out to meet somewhere convenient—this was of course one way. But on second thought it would hardly do: Brother Zuoxing had told me to my face that of late he seemed to feel he had been marked and followed, though he could not yet be sure of it; and, to be cautious, had already been told to suspend his activity for the time. For this reason it seemed best not to trouble him.

I dialled a call to Brother Zuoxing, meaning to make sure I had the wireless station’s address aright; but the bell rang several times with no one to answer—asleep, perhaps, and soundly—and so I would trouble him no further.
Some forty-odd minutes past four, a mighty force took command of me: I resolved to go myself!

It was the season of the Double Ninth, and morning and evening already carried a fair chill; I put on a full suit of Western clothes, and over it a lined overcoat. Back in the bedroom I looked upon my wife and children: my wife had not lain down, and though the wool was still in her hands, she watched my every movement with fixed attention. She asked me, “You are going out?” I comforted her: “I’ll go to one place first, and then find Old Qi; nothing should come of it. By eight at the latest I’ll surely telephone home; wait here, and on no account go out.” She nodded, and helplessly laid down her knitting.

Softly I opened the bedroom door, turned the corner, then slowly twisted the knob and drew back the front door, and stepped out to the lane-mouth. The street lay hushed and still, not a passer-by upon it. The dim street-lamps threw their light upon the ground in one gray, dingy sheet.

At that time there were three wireless stations that kept up regular communication between “Shanghai District” and Chongqing; the nearest to my dwelling on Seymour Road was on Sinza Road—no need of a tram, nor any to be had, and a few minutes’ walk brought one there.

As I went, one hand thrust in my overcoat pocket gripped five dollars: should I meet a patrolling constable, then by my dress alone a question or two would be the most of it, and enough to see me off. As it fell, all was quiet along the way, and I met with nothing.

This station was on the fourth floor—the topmost—of an apartment house, with windows giving on the street; I looked up and saw the “safety mark” all in order, and so went up on soft feet. I knocked twice, one light, one heavy; no one answered. I waited a while, and knocked twice more; still no response. I began to feel uneasy—surely not? Sound asleep, perhaps? Even to dress and rise takes some little time, the more so in the dead of night. I looked at my watch: ten past five. In the midst of my doubting there came a faint stir within; and before my eyes the door opened the smallest crack. Someone within was looking at me; the light was dim, yet one could make it out. Looking in, I seemed to see a black glass bead glinting in the crack of the door—who it was I could not in the least tell; and if it were the enemy “lying in wait,” then I could only own myself beaten.

The door opened, and it was none other than the chief operator—styled the station chief as well—×××. (The three station chiefs of “Shanghai District” were Comrades Qin Ertong, Zhang Xiangnan, and Gu Hanqing; which of them this station’s was, I could still have told a few years ago, but now dare not be certain who.) With no time for anything else, I hastily drafted a telegram reporting the emergency, and asked him to send it at once in the station’s cipher-book. He told me that the next hour for transmission was not until seven. I was minded to wait and see it sent before I went; but on second thought there would be no immediate reply, nor any need to waste more time here, and it was of more pressing urgency to see Old Qi and settle how to meet the spreading blaze. So I begged the station chief to take the further trouble, once he had transmitted, of asking Chongqing to grant a little more time for communication with Shanghai.

It was not yet half past five, and the sky not yet light, when I was again walking, solitary, along the street. As I went I turned it over: I must find a taxi garage. There was one, as I recalled, not far off—the Xiangsheng—and rounding one more street-corner I came to it. As ill luck would have it, there were cars but no drivers, and I could only wait with patience; after some five minutes an empty car at last came back. I got in, and first pressed two dollars on the driver (the short fare was, as I recall, one dollar), and bade him take me to the French Concession, opposite the Lyceum Theater.

The way was not far, and the passage unhindered; in a few minutes I was at the Lyceum Theater. I got down, and let the car go on—there was nothing to fear in that. Again I sharpened my wariness and, with all my wits about me, scanned the neighborhood round about: not so much as a man’s shadow, nor anything worth a second look. The Lyceum Theater stands on Rue Bourgeat; turning left from the theater’s great door—whether this street too is called Rue Bourgeat, I cannot now recall.

I went of set purpose to the far side of the street, and looked up at the third floor of this house into which Brother Qi Qingbin had newly moved: though a thick curtain hung across the window, it could not shut in the light of the lamp within. Strange—why should the lamp be lit at such an hour?

Moving my steps slowly, I walked on, then turned my head aside to look closely at the hard card set beneath the window-lattice: just then, from the lamplight, one could see the shadow it cast—did that not signify all was safe?

I was on the point of stepping across the street when a second thought came: no—Old Qi would not rise before dawn, nor sit up wakeful to the first light of day without sleeping; better be careful. So I quickened my pace and walked straight on. I heeded all about me: not the least sign of anything amiss.

As I walked, it came to me: Old Qi had two children, who must rise early for school, and his little maid-servant must get their breakfast ready and see to their dressing and washing and the rest—how could she do it in the dark? Was this not the best explanation of the lamp’s being lit?

To be sure! Old Qi had moved here but two or three days since, and even the courier had not yet been in touch with him; when we had met here a dozen-odd hours before, we had spoken of this very point, and to his own sense there was nothing to suspect. Moreover, even Pockface—Brother Zhang Zuoxing—whom we met with often, had never been here, because he stood suspected of “carrying the germ,” and for fear of any infection had been kept away. Think as I might, this way and that, surely nothing could have gone wrong.
There was no need to hesitate longer; I turned about, crossed the street, and went straight toward Old Qi’s dwelling.

Looking up again at the third floor, the lamplight there was as before, with no sight of any moving shadow of a person; I made a point of pausing a moment at the foot of the stairs, and bent my ear to listen—no response of any kind. All these motions were as though I were frightening my own self.
No need to waver: I resolved to go up.

This was a new house of the apartment kind, its staircase not too narrow. Climbing to the first turning after nine steps, I saw a rattan chair set there—hullo! was there a night-watchman in this house too? I looked again at the floor: no cigarette-ends, no burnt matchsticks, nothing of the sort—what was one to make of it? Could someone have kept watch here? Yet I could not, for want of an answer, turn on my heel and go down again.

Letting it be, I turned on up the stairs, past the second floor, where I found nothing out of the way, and so mounted to the third. Not three or five steps from the stairhead—here it was. Again I looked to left and right: no one, and no stir.

By our agreement I put out my right hand, and with my forefinger pressed the bell—two short, one long. The bell had scarcely ceased when out from the crack of the door there reached a hand; I saw it clearly—a woman’s hand—which shook twice quickly and drew back. A shiver ran through me despite myself; my heart gave a great start, and on the instant I turned and leapt down the stairs, my very breath near stopped, and felt my two legs go somewhat weak beneath me.

By the time I had reached the great door, three steps at a bound, I heard behind me, from above, the sound of heavy leather shoes come leaping and clattering down in pursuit. I had no time to look back and see who it was, still less to reckon whether it were one man or two or three. I ran out of the door, turned right, and sped at a headlong run toward the Lyceum Theater, my heart on its guard lest the pursuers fire to stop me, and half-unwittingly holding a zigzag “Z” course as I went. In truth this was all superfluous—it did but slacken my speed, and would cost me my balance besides.

Just as I had run past the door of the Lyceum Theater, and was making to turn into a lane, the man behind was already no great way from me. In my flurry, the lined overcoat I wore caught—of all things—on a telegraph-pole; I gave it a hard wrench, all but pitching over, and by the time I had steadied my feet and made to run on, my pursuer had come up: I felt only a heavy blow upon the calf of my leg, and on the instant lost my balance, and could not but plunge headlong, coming down flat on my face with both hands to the ground. My pursuer, taking his advantage, dropped his whole weight rump-first upon my spine, and struggle as I might, I could stir no more.

Their men were more than one: the one who came up after and the one who had pinned me down, one to my left and one to my right, the two of them together braced me up and lifted me from the ground; and sure enough, each had a pistol in his hand.

Done for—all was done for; a false judgment had made me a great fool for all my cleverness. These two men were neither of them tall, thick-set and stoutly built, and from first to last never opened their mouths to say a word. I had seen it long since—they were both Japanese. One of them twisted my arm up behind my back, and now and again bore down hard upon it; the other held his pistol-mouth against my waist, and so, gripping me, they walked me toward the very house where Old Qi lived. By this time the sky was paling, though the sun had not yet shown its face.

It was not that I hung back and would not go, but that they liked to shove and jostle, and so crowded me up to the third floor. In the room was yet another little fellow, keeping watch over the young maid with her plaited hair—she, perhaps, was the very A-ping who had waved her hand in warning through the crack of the door?

I could not see Old Qi, nor Sister Qi his wife; even the children were nowhere to be seen. A-ping’s face was all sorrow and dread, and the whole room hung thick with a foul, smothering air. Much I longed to throw all to the winds and ask A-ping what in truth had happened—no; to open my mouth would be to betray a flaw; better first to observe coolly a while, and then take my course.

Now I saw it: these three had been left behind to “lie in wait,” and Old Qi, I feared, had already been carried off by them. The two who had just now given chase were most likely Japanese gendarmes in plain clothes; and the little short man keeping guard in the room was, perhaps, the interpreter. This one wore a wooden, expressionless face, his two eyes squinting sidelong at me as he weighed up who I might be; and the moment they met my gaze he turned his head hastily aside—a very type of the mean and rat-faced sort. The two who had chased me muttered a few words to one side, and then one of them went out.

They had not put handcuffs on me—why they were so “open-handed” I did not know; could it be they still could not fathom just what I was about? I sat in the seat pointed out to me in the sitting-room; the Japanese who had kicked me and dropped his weight upon me sat, pistol in hand, on a chair some three or four feet from me, and watched me without a blink, as though, should I but stir, he would fire on the instant.

I steadied my breath a little and set to laying a plan. Since they did not know me, they could not of course make out my identity; and were I to put them off with talk of the sort that I had come to the wrong place, I feared it would be of no avail. Better frankly own that I was a “courier” doing the work of passing messages, and so for the moment mask and cover my true identity, the better to watch for a chance to act. As it was now, I could but deal with it as far as it would go.

My spirits a little easier, my mouth all flat and stale, I longed greatly for a cigarette. I was just reaching for my pocket when I hastily drew my hand back, and said to the little short man: “Here—this one—I should like to smoke; there are some in my pocket. May I take them myself? Set your minds at rest, I have no gun on me.” At this his brows shot up, and he came over at once, reached in to turn out my pockets, felt me up and down a few times more, and only then took out the cigarettes and set them on the table not far from me. I took one, and he lit it for me with a lighter—the two of us playing out, just so, a scene of dumb-show.

A pull at the cigarette, and my mouth turned dry; I wanted water again, and said, “My mouth is parched; would you have that young maid bring me a cup of water?” That cup of plain boiled water was of a savour beyond telling—truly it was both good to drink and quenched the thirst. I watched their every motion with care, but could get no answer from it. Just at this moment several men pushed in at the door; and besides the Japanese who had gone out a while before, the foremost of them, in Western coat and leather shoes, all airs and swagger, first split his mouth in a smile at me—which did but make me find him the more hateful—and then said to me in Cantonese-accented Mandarin: “What work is it you do? You had best make a clean breast of it; if you don’t tell the truth, mind you’ll taste some bitterness.” Coming out from the first with this threatening tone, bidding me speak out, he was plainly a hard customer to deal with. I had no course but to fall in with his drift, and answered in his own vein: “What I do, of course, is no secret from you; to tell the truth, I am an anti-Japanese man sent from Chongqing—” I had got but this far when he lost patience: “I am asking what post you hold.” So I went straight on: “I am the internal courier here.” He asked next, “What is your name?” I said, “My surname is Zhang—the Zhang written with ‘stand’ over ‘early’—and my name is Zhang Baozhao.” He pressed further:

“What have you come here to do?” I said, “I came to fetch a letter.” He glared at me, and there let it drop. He and the few who had come with him put their heads together, whispering I know not what, and then with a wave of the hand signed to me to stand up and go along with them.

Two cars stood at the door; the little Cantonese hauled me up into the rear one, and another squeezed in after, so that I was wedged just in the middle of the back seat. The driver seemed to be in a settled understanding with them; he did not so much as ask where to go, but started off and drove swiftly away.
I could not make out the sights outside the car, nor knew where we were being driven; and I thought—this, surely, was my last look upon it all!

I marked the direction as we went: the car headed neither north nor west, and after five or six minutes it stopped. Looking up, I saw it was the French Concession central police station. They marched me up the high steps and into a spacious hall, where, as in some doctor’s waiting-room, a good many people already sat about. As I looked round the circle, my eye fell at once on the tall figure of Old Qi among them; his face was worn and haggard, and in the one night his cheeks had grown all black with stubble. I fixed my eyes on him, and he too opened his eyes wide and gazed at me—in his look there were surprise, disappointment, chagrin, and bitter hatred, all together, only that he had no fit way to speak them out.

I sat in the middle of a row of straight-backed chairs, set sideways over against Brother Qingbin, and much hoped to read in his eyes, or in some small motion, a clue of some kind; but somehow, for the moment, my wits were dull past all bearing.

Old Qi and I, but yesterday, had been together talking of this and that, weighing over the great affairs of the world; who could have thought that in a single night, to exchange even a few words was hemmed in by our circumstances—for us, it might be called a sudden turn of wind and cloud! Yet things had come to such a pass, and sighing would mend nothing of the fact; better to gather my spirit to meet the many hard problems soon to come.

Amid the din of voices, another party crowded into the hall; my eyes started, and I near cried out in alarm—of a sudden I saw that my wife too had been seized and brought in. Heedless of all else, I stood up at once and hurried forward to catch her hand, asking, “Was it that you saw I did not come home, and went to the Qi house to look for me?” She nodded, and I warned her: “Say as little as you possibly can—” I had got but this far when someone came over to interfere, and at the same time dragged me back to my former seat. I would not sit, but raised my voice and said to the little Cantonese: “This lady is my wife; you see, she is big with child, and no worker either—what do you seize her for? Did I, Zhang Baozhao, not tell you just now that I am the internal courier? Whatever you would ask, ask me, and on no account harass her.” These few words, though on the face of them an appeal to reason and feeling, were in truth a hint dropped for Old Qi and my wife to hear—so that later they should not each tell a different tale, and the flaws grow ever wider. But this little Cantonese held his peace, and with a smile that was no smile looked away elsewhere. Just then the wall-clock in the hall—the waiting-room for the examination—pointed to twenty-seven minutes past eight; and from another room a man came out and called Old Qi to follow him in. Old Qi rose, seeming very weary—perhaps because he was so tall, his very back was a little bowed—yet he kept still a high composure. What could put fresh heart in me was that the men of the station would not let the Japanese go in after him. I thought, when by and by it came my turn to go in, and it were the same, then there would be some small chance yet to be turned to use.

Old Qi, called within, came out again in but a dozen-odd minutes; from his look one could make out nothing. Then it came to my turn, and, sure enough, they would not let the little Cantonese follow behind; though the men wrangled a few words over it, in the end it was I who went in alone.

This was an office, and not, as one had fancied, with a judge enthroned on high looking sternly down to question. Behind the large writing-desk sat a Frenchman, about fifty, short and squarely built, neither slow nor hurried, a man of much quality; I hoped he might be Malone, the contact of our “Shanghai District.” Beside the desk sat another Chinese, younger than he, a cardboard folder before him—by the look of it, either a clerk or an interpreter. The foreigner waved me to the empty seat set ready, meaning, no doubt, to ask me a few things. Without waiting for his question, I rashly called out first, “Monsieur Malone,” to see whether he would show any response; and unlooked-for, he smilingly nodded. Then he said a few words in some foreign tongue I could not follow to the young Chinese, who glanced at me, rose, and went off behind through another door.

Whether this man—Malone, it might be—understood what I said or no, I cared not, but told him straight what was in my heart; and to make it the easier for him, I spoke and made signs together: “I am ‘Guanzhen,’ the man in charge in Shanghai.” I paused, and with my eyes asked him whether he understood; he nodded again and again. I asked him further, “What can you do for me?”—and hard upon it added, “Can you not keep me here?” He shook his head hard, and pointed with his finger to the telephone on the desk. Taking his meaning, I stepped forward, picked it up, and dialled; Malone glanced outside. I heard the bell ring at the other end, but no one answered; unwilling to give up, I hung up, took it again, and rang once more—it was the voice of Sister ——. I said, “Is the gentleman in?” She said, “He is in the washroom.” I said, “Quick—ask him to come and take it at once.” This was the last command I was to give out before I had lost my freedom by a hundred parts in the hundred. “Hello! Old Qi and I bid you good-bye; Cheng Yuan goes too. From now on the whole charge is yours—report it out at once, send word to each apart, await instructions, and shift your quarters.” Without waiting for the other to speak I hung up on the instant, for fear of being caught out. This call had gone to the “Second Office,” and the one who answered was the personnel assistant secretary, Gui Difei.

I went back to my former seat; and though I knew well that Malone could be of no great help, yet, standing now at the very pass of life and death, I hoped still that he might think of some way—that I be not delivered to the “Japanese gendarmerie” or to “No. 76.” So I asked Malone again to contrive to help; Malone rose from the desk and turned to go off behind. Just at this moment someone put his head in at the door, made as if to enter, then seemed to be stopped. After two or three minutes Malone came back together with the young man of before, spread his two hands at me, showing a face of utter helplessness—and there was no help for it then.

Driven to seek the next best, I raised my voice a little and said to Malone: “You see, my wife too has been seized and brought here; she is not only with child, but has two children at home besides, and has moreover nothing whatever to do with the work we do—on grounds of humanity, you ought to set her free to go home at once. As for me—since you have bowed to the authority of the Japanese, I can but leave myself to you.” Malone and the man spoke a long while in French, and the man passed it on to me: “He says he feels for you deeply, but that he and his superiors alike, he fears, can do nothing to help, and so he tenders you his ten-thousandfold apology. As to the matter of your lady, he undertakes to press the Japanese hard for it, and will go now to treat with them.”

So saying, Malone went out again. In this way near half an hour more had passed; and the fellow who spoke Cantonese, seeming to weary of the wait, now put his head in to look, now made to burst in, till even the constables grew plainly disgusted with him.
After Malone came back, the interpreter told me: “Your wife may go home; but you gentlemen must put up with hardship.” What? “You gentlemen”? Then who else was there, besides Old Qi and me?

The time was past nine on the morning of the thirtieth of the tenth month of the thirtieth year of the Republic. Old Qi in front and I behind, with yet another I could not make out, we were crowded out of the French police station, each of us braced along by two men. I would have said a few words to my wife, but they seemed not to hear; heedless of them, as I walked I told her aloud: “When you get home, go nowhere—just wait for word of me.” And having said these two sentences, I could not but be downcast for it.
It was the same car as before; Old Qi and I, like the two slabs of meat in a sandwich, were pressed in tight, unable to stir at all, near squeezed till we could not draw breath.
The car had but two possible bournes: one, the gendarmerie at Zhabei; the other, “No. 76” in western Shanghai. We had not long started when it was to be judged we were heading west.

Several times in the car Old Qi made to speak; his lips would tremble a moment, yet no sound came out—forced down, it may be, by main strength. I too wished to speak, my aim being to get our tales to tally; but they were neither fools nor dolts, and it was best to hold silent. Better to watch their words and read their looks, and learn as much as ever I could—it might make me the fitter to cope.

Looking out of the car, my line of sight was all screened by the men aboard, and I could see nothing clearly. Old Qi went so far as to shut his eyes; I would not shut mine—I meant to see, and see plainly.

Before long the car slowed and stopped; we had reached a certain place. The little Cantonese jumped down first, and the sentry at the gate saluted him; at a word from him, the cars all drove on inside. Not far within the gate, a turn to the left, and the car stopped again; and besides Old Qi and me, even the driver aboard came tumbling helter-skelter down, and stood at once to either side, and bade us get out.

At this moment I saw there were yet two more cars, with men aboard them too, though none could be seen to get down. They led the way, and we passed through a small side door, within which was something like a passage—or one might call it a courtyard—with a row of single-storey houses ranged along either side, north and south, all partitioned off into little rooms. Old Qi they took into the middle one of those facing north with their backs to the south; me they took into another. The room was meanly furnished, a table and chairs of wood and nothing more. Now, surely, the “interrogation” was to come; and I could not but feel a fit of bitter helplessness.

The one who came in was still the man of the Cantonese accent. He asked me whether I was hungry, and would I have a bowl of noodles; but I could get nothing down, and what I most felt the need of was a cup of water. Beyond all looking-for, he not only did not question me, but made me a little speech of self-introduction: “My name is Lin Huanzhi; I am now in charge of the action section here. In former days I was of the Fourth Team of ‘Shanghai District,’ and my elder brother Lin Zhencheng was in the Third Team. No need for many words—I hope that from ‘old colleagues’ we may become ‘new colleagues,’ and all will be well.” By his tone he plainly did not know my identity; and though my belly was full of fire, I must of course hold my temper down and play the “courier” through to the end.

Lin Huanzhi opened with a trap: “I don’t take you for a courier.” I made no answer, and he went on: “What charge do you hold? Best speak it out plainly, or none of us will be easy.” I said, “Section-Chief Lin, since I am come to this place, what is there I could keep hidden from you? I think it were better you let me and that tall fellow have a talk first—I cannot, at any rate, slip out of the palm of your hand.” He hesitated somewhat; and just at this moment in came another man, half a head shorter than Lin Huanzhi, an olive-shaped face, a snake’s waist, two great eyes, a cigarette dangling from a mouth like an old woman’s—no pleasant sight at all. It struck me of a sudden: could this fellow be the very Wan Lilang?

Lin Huanzhi rose to greet the man, and the two whispered a word or two in a corner, upon which this man turned and went out again. Only then did Lin Huanzhi make answer to my request of a moment since to speak with Old Qi. In a warning tone he said, “Talk you may, but play no tricks.” So saying, he took me to the next room. Old Qi sat there with bowed head, and by the look of him had suffered no ill-usage.

Lin Huanzhi, of set purpose, kept out of the way—there might, for aught I knew, be someone listening in secret. So I drew close to Old Qi and said low: “They do not yet know who I am; I have said I am the internal courier Zhang Baozhao, and hope to pass muster for a while, and look later for a chance.” Old Qi shook his head, meaning it was no good plan. I asked again, “And you, then?” Old Qi said, “They have it all clear and plain already; whatever comes, just push it all onto me alone.” The words were not out before Lin Huanzhi came in to bid me go with him.

This time it was not to the next room; we went out at the corner door, turned right, and there seemed to be a great drill-ground, straight on to the far end of which stood a tall foreign-style house. Just so—the “High Foreign House” spoken of in the intelligence reports; this, most likely, was the place. Up the high steps—some seven or eight of them; and outside the great hall stood again two armed guards. Going in, on the right, was a reception-room set with eight or nine great sofas, a dark, dense press of them, and an air of deathly gloom about it.

That unpleasing fellow was already waiting there, and said with all his airs: “My name is Wan Lilang. Let me first make one or two friends known to you, and then we’ll talk.” I said within myself: “The scoundrelly turtle’s egg, sure enough—to think of falling into the hands of a beast in man’s clothes like this; I could not close my eyes in death.” Ah—he said he would make friends known to me; what did that mean? Was it that he would fetch someone to identify me?

I had not guessed amiss: Chu Yapeng came in from outside. At first, his boyishness not yet shed, he wore his old grinning, giggling look; but the moment he caught sight of me, it was as though he had touched a live wire, and he stood there stock-still. Wan Lilang pointed at me and asked him, “Have you seen him before?” Chu Yapeng hesitated the briefest instant, then quickly shook his head; and Wan Lilang turned the question back on me. I answered, “This is Mr. Chu.” Then I said further to Chu Yapeng: “Mr. Chu, you may not call it to mind, but two months ago—did I not carry goods to that electrical shop at the corner on Bubbling Well Road?” This I said on purpose for Wan to hear, to show I was a courier; but by his look he did not lightly believe the tale.

In truth Chu Yapeng had at first been a courier of the “Beiping station,” transferred to Shanghai, his work the same as before; and because he was fond of assembling wireless sets, he had later taken over a little shop-front on Bubbling Well Road and opened an electrical shop there, to serve as a point of liaison for “Shanghai District,” and left it in Chu Yapeng’s charge. Better than a month before, Chu had been arrested, his case unclear; yet the electrical shop was still open there and doing its business as usual—used already, it might be, by the enemy and the puppets. That today he had not pointed me out showed he had a conscience still, when all was said.

Chu Yapeng sat to one side, and in came Jiang Anhua too—he was commander of the “Shanghai District Third Action Brigade,” and had been under arrest some while now; had I not seen him here, I should not even have known whether he were alive or dead. His clothes were in disorder, his hair a tangle, his cheeks all stubble, a mildewed ill-luck upon his whole face—one look, and you knew he had come out of a cell. He stood there without a flicker of expression, of set purpose keeping his eyes turned from me; and when Wan Lilang bade him sit, he was but then casting about how to meet this awkward pass that he had never looked for.
I thought within me, this was bad: if one after another they were brought to know me, sooner or later a flaw must show. And in truth the flaws were already not a few.

Wan Lilang asked Jiang Anhua of a sudden, “Do you two know each other well?” Jiang shook his head—shook it with some little reluctance, so that not Wan Lilang alone could see it, but even I felt it boded ill. At this Wan Lilang wore an air of no small triumph; yet he pressed the question no further.

Two more men came in from outside; the foremost of them, fat and round of face, a pair of dark glasses astride his nose, wore a smile as he gave place to the man behind. I looked hard—and the man behind was none other than Qian Xinmin, the District Chief of our “Nanjing District”; and now here was trouble indeed. Before I could make any sign, he had got in a step ahead, caught my hand, and cried out loud, “Brother Gongshu!”—then, with his other hand as well, shaking it and calling over and over, “Brother Gongshu! Brother Gongshu!”

Qian Xinmin’s one cry pierced through my true identity, and broke off my last thread of hope; there was, of course, no more need to play the “courier.” And so I rose abruptly, pulled the lined overcoat from my back and flung it over the back of the sofa, set my necktie straight with a motion of my hand, and said, with a grave face, to Wan Lilang: “Quite right—I am Chen Gongshu, Chief of ‘Shanghai District.’”

Things being come to this, my once-strained feelings grew, on the contrary, a good deal easier; I felt myself the steadier, too, in meeting the many problems soon to come. First: I knew that come what might, I must not lose the dignity that becomes a District Chief; as for how they meant to deal with me, that was their affair. Second: this was no simple, single matter of one man; though I had lost the power to command, it was yet my duty to guard the safety of the organization, and to see that its people, a thousand strong, could go on with their work.

To speak frankly, I had at that time no wish merely to seek a quick death—else I should not have lived to this day. And why would I not die? Because I had lost too cheaply, and meant to win my stakes back again.

If one should use the words “to bear disgrace and cling to life” to describe this passage of my story, I cannot but own them; yet in fact it was not wholly so, for there were indeed within it certain turns of fortune beyond all looking-for. In the next book, whatever I passed through—be it to my credit or to my blackening—I shall set down without the least disguise, and keep back nothing; and though this will call up many a bitter memory, yet to be able thereby to keep the truth is, after all, more easeful to the heart than to dress up a front and make up a set of false tales.

Last of all, one point I must make plain: this defeat can be reckoned no more than a stumble of my own horse; the Shanghai work under the leadership of the “Juntong Bureau” was not, for my dereliction, broken off. It is learned that after “Shanghai District” had suffered its grievous ruin, the whole charge was taken up by Brother Jiang Shaomo (Cilie)—Chief of the “Shanghai Reserve District” (also called the Second District), who had lain hidden in Shanghai and never once let his identity be exposed—and that he fought on unremitting until the victory of the war of resistance.
